title: Ask what's needed
hookLine: good service asks first instead of assuming

cards: After big disasters, something strange can happen. People far away want to help, so they pack boxes, old coats, canned food, stuffed animals, and ship them off. And the boxes pile up.
Relief workers have to sort them, store them, sometimes throw them away, while what the place actually needed was clean water, cash, or a specific medicine.
Some aid workers have a grim nickname for it: the second disaster. Every one of those boxes was packed with love. But nobody had asked the people on the ground.

teach.b: There's a small, striking scene in the Gospel of Mark. Jesus is leaving the town of Jericho, and a blind man named Bartimaeus sits by the road, shouting for help. The crowd tells him to be quiet.
Jesus stops, calls him over, and asks a question that sounds almost odd: "What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?" The need seems obvious. The man is blind.
But Jesus asks anyway, and Bartimaeus answers in his own words: that I might receive my sight. Whatever you make of the story, there's a lesson in the asking.
It treats the person as the expert on their own life. It doesn't assume. The same idea runs through modern service, in a very different setting.
In the disability rights movement, a slogan spread in the nineteen nineties: nothing about us without us. Don't design for people without asking them.
Some aid groups now give cash instead, so people can choose what they need themselves. And it scales all the way down to your kitchen. A friend has a new baby.
You could bring lasagna, and that might be lovely.
Or you could ask, and learn that what they really want is someone to walk the dog, or hold the baby for an hour so they can shower. Asking takes a little humility; it admits you don't already know.
But it turns help from something you give into something you do together.

how: Some relief organizations ask communities what they need, or give cash so people can choose, and volunteer programs often train helpers to ask before acting.

games.q: you're Jesus in Mark's story. a blind man calls out to you by the road. what do you do first?
o: heal him at once; the need is obvious.
games.why: he asks, What wilt thou that I should do unto thee? even an obvious need gets a question, and the man answers in his own words.

practice: Think of someone going through something, a new job, an illness, a move, a loss, and notice what you assumed they need. Now set that assumption down.
Picture yourself asking, simply, what would actually help right now, and waiting for the answer, even if it surprises you.

carryVoice: Your line: ask first. The person you're helping is the expert on their own life. Until tomorrow.
